title: RVT Study Guide - Comprehensive Supplement
description: Detailed study materials extracted from Vascular Study Guide 2 - comprehensive exam preparation for Registered Vascular Technologist certification

Cerebrovascular.title: Cerebrovascular System - Detailed Study
keyFacts: Carotid exam performed with patient supine, neck slightly extended, head turned away from side being scanned
ICA = Internal Carotid Artery (low resistance vessel)
ECA = External Carotid Artery (high resistance vessel)
Vertebral arteries evaluated as part of cerebrovascular assessment
70-99% carotid stenosis is a CRITICAL FINDING requiring immediate attention
Linear array transducer used for carotid exams
Most common reason for underestimation of carotid stenosis = improper sample volume location
Cursor should be placed at narrowest point of stenosis initially
Move Doppler cursor through entire stenotic area to find highest velocity
Bruit can be heard with stenosis, also with branching/tortuosity
normalValues: ICA has increased acceleration time (AT) compared to high resistance vessels due to low resistance
AT longer in ICA and cerebral vessels vs extremity arteries
ICA waveform: low resistance with continuous forward diastolic flow
ECA waveform: high resistance with minimal/reversed diastolic flow
pathologyFindings: Carotid stenosis: 50% diameter = 75% area stenosis = hemodynamically significant
Increased PSV and EDV at stenosis site
Post-stenotic turbulence (eddy currents/vortices) distal to stenosis
diagnosticCriteria: 50% diameter stenosis = 75% area stenosis = hemodynamically significant
70-99% stenosis = critical finding requiring immediate attention
ICA/CCA velocity ratio helpful for grading stenosis
scanningTechnique: Patient supine with neck slightly extended
Head turned away from side being scanned
Scan entire length of CCA, ICA, ECA, and vertebral arteries
Multiple angles through stenosis to find peak velocity
Sample volume centered in vessel at narrowest point

ArterialHemodynamics.title: Arterial Hemodynamics - Detailed Study

characteristics: Late diastole: small amount of forward flow
Seen in high resistance vascular beds (extremities/muscles)
Diastole: some retrograde flow (less than triphasic)
Loss of late diastolic forward component
Can be normal in older patients
ABNORMAL if seen in organ vessels

monophasic.description: Low resistance or significant proximal disease
characteristics: Antegrade flow continues through entire cardiac cycle
Normal in vessels feeding organs (low resistance)
ABNORMAL if seen in extremity arteries
monophasic.significance: Normal for organs, ABNORMAL for extremities (indicates significant proximal disease or vasodilation)

tardusParvus.significance: Indicates severe proximal stenosis or occlusion

keyPoints: Increases at stenosis site due to body maintaining blood volume
Measured at narrowest point of stenosis
Velocity increases as vessel diameter decreases
Continuity principle: flow volume remains constant
Low in high resistance beds, higher in low resistance

highResistance: Triphasic waveforms with retrograde diastolic flow
Minimal or no forward diastolic flow
Clenching fist increases distal resistance and pulsatility in proximal arteries
lowResistance: Supplies organs needing constant blood flow
Monophasic waveforms with continuous forward flow
Examples: ICA, renal, mesenteric, hepatic arteries

physiologicEffects: Cold patient: vasoconstriction increases arterial resistance
Warm patient: vasodilation decreases arterial resistance
Exercise: vasodilation in muscles, increased flow
Fist clenching: increases resistance, more pulsatile proximally
Upon fist release: resistance drops, pulsatility reduced, flow increases
cardiacFactors: Decreased cardiac function = decreased output = reduced peak arterial velocities
Increased cardiac function = increased output = increased peak arterial velocities
Cardiac output affects all arterial velocities systemically
Velocity ratios help normalize for cardiac output variations

positioning: Supine or semi-erect (if breathing problems/vertigo/back pain)
Knee slightly bent, leg abducted for medial aspect access
Decubitus/lateral for popliteal fossa and posterior calf access
normalCharacteristics: Triphasic waveforms in healthy extremity arteries
Pulsatility Index increases with distance from aorta

hemodynamicSignificance: 50% diameter stenosis = 75% area stenosis = hemodynamically significant
effectsOfStenosis: Proximal to stenosis: dampened flow velocity with increased resistance
At stenosis: increased velocity (blood escaping stenotic area)
Proximal and distal: increased velocities detected
Pressure drop at stenosis with increased velocity (Bernoulli effect)
Decreased resistance and velocity distal to stenosis

pathophysiology: Arterioles already dilated at rest when stenosis present
Ankle pressure drops with exercise in PAD
Ischemic symptoms in muscles during exercise
findings: Tardus parvus waveforms distal to severe stenosis

aneurysms.definition: Permanent focal dilation of artery >50% normal diameter
types: True aneurysm: involves all 3 vessel layers
Pseudoaneurysm: contained rupture with fibrous capsule
Saccular: affects one side of vessel wall

acute: 6 P's: Pain, Pallor, Pulselessness, Paresthesia, Paralysis, Poikilothermia
chronic: NOT critical due to collateral circulation

causes: Improper sample volume location near wall
interpretation: Laminar flow = narrow bandwidth, clear spectral window
Turbulent flow = wide bandwidth, filled spectral window

spontaneousFlow: Should be present in CFV, femoral, popliteal veins
Calf veins and saphenous veins normally do NOT demonstrate spontaneity
respiratoryPhasicity: Flow moves from high to low pressure
Lower extremities - Inspiration: decreased intrathoracic pressure, increased intra-abdominal pressure → decreased flow
Lower extremities - Expiration: increased intrathoracic pressure, decreased intra-abdominal pressure → increased flow toward heart
Upper extremities - Inspiration: increased flow toward heart
Loss of phasicity suggests proximal obstruction
cardiacPulsatility: Causes turbulent flow in upper vena cava, upper arms, hepatic veins
NORMAL in upper extremities and hepatic veins
ABNORMAL if seen in lower extremities = indicates CHF (Congestive Heart Failure)
augmentation: Tests patency between compression site and probe
reflux: Retrograde flow lasting >0.5-1.0 seconds indicates incompetence

normal: Competent valves allow unidirectional flow toward heart
Flow moves from superficial to deep system through perforators
Valves close due to hydrostatic pressure preventing retrograde flow

principles: Weight of blood column in vessels
Proportional to height of blood column
Zero at heart level in all positions
values: Pressure increases below heart, decreases above heart

normal: Calf muscle pump decreases venous pressure with walking
abnormal: With incompetent valves: remains at ~100mmHg (standing pressure)
Pressure does not drop adequately with exercise

VenousAnatomy.title: Venous Anatomy - Detailed Study
deepVeins: Carry majority of blood back to heart (85-90%)
Include: CFV, femoral, popliteal, tibial veins

GSV: Evaluated with patient standing (preferably on stool)
Leg rotated outward for medial aspect access
Most common site for venous insufficiency
Runs from medial ankle to saphenofemoral junction
SSV: Evaluated with patient seated at bed edge, legs dependent
Joins popliteal vein at knee (saphenopopliteal junction)
characteristics: Connect to deep system via perforators

perforators: Connect superficial to deep venous system
Flow from superficial to deep during muscle relaxation
Flow from deep to superficial during muscle contraction (normal)
Incompetent perforators allow reflux from deep to superficial
Contribute to varicose veins when incompetent

DVTEvaluation: Veins more easily visualized when distended

principles: Complete compression = vein completely collapses = patent
Use adequate pressure but not excessive
transmuralpressure: Flattened veins with low volume: low transmural pressure
Low transmural pressure = more resistance to flow, LESS resistance to compression
Circular veins with higher volume: high transmural pressure
High transmural pressure = less resistance to flow, MORE resistance to compression
Semi-erect positioning distends veins for better visualization

spontaneity: Assess if flow is present without augmentation
Should be present in large veins (CFV, femoral, popliteal)
Calf veins may not show spontaneity normally
Absence in large veins suggests obstruction
phasicity: Loss of phasicity suggests proximal obstruction
Different pattern in upper vs lower extremities
augmentation: Tests patency between compression and probe
reflux: Must be evaluated in standing position

criticalFindings: Free-floating thrombus tail (not adhered to wall) = CRITICAL - high embolism risk

pathophysiology: CVI: remains at ~100mmHg or higher with walking

normal: Venous pressure drops with ambulation to ~30mmHg
dysfunction: Causes: muscle wasting, obstruction, incompetent valves
Venous pressure decreases only slightly with ambulation

ABI.description: Ankle-Brachial Index - compares ankle pressure to brachial pressure
normalFindings: Ankle and brachial pressures equal or ankle slightly higher
Normal: ankle pressure same or higher than arm at rest
Exercise: pressures remain same or increase slightly
abnormalFindings: Exercise causes ankle pressure to drop with arterial disease
Reduced ABI indicates peripheral arterial disease
ABI.calculation: ABI = Highest ankle pressure / Highest brachial pressure

purpose: Pressure gradient >20mmHg between segments = significant stenosis

PVR.description: Pulse Volume Recording - measures volume changes in limb segment

normalResponse: Flow increases 3-5x resting flow with exercise
Ankle/brachial pressures same or mildly increased after exercise
Arterioles dilate to meet muscle oxygen demand
abnormalResponse: With stenosis: arterioles already dilated at rest
Cannot further reduce resistance with exercise
Muscles cannot increase flow to meet demand

PhysicsInstrumentation.title: Physics & Instrumentation - Detailed Study

basics: Doppler effect: frequency shift when sound reflects from moving object
Flow toward transducer = positive frequency shift (above baseline)
Flow away from transducer = negative frequency shift (below baseline)
Frequency shift proportional to blood velocity
dopplerPrinciples.dopplerEquation: Frequency shift = (2 × velocity × transmitted frequency × cos angle) / speed of sound

principles: At 90°: cos(90°) = 0, no Doppler shift detected
Larger angles = greater error in velocity calculation
Angle correction cursor must be parallel to vessel wall/blood flow
errors: Most common cause of velocity measurement error
Angle correction line must align with flow direction

aliasing.description: Occurs when velocity exceeds Nyquist limit (PRF/2)
spectralDoppler: Appears on opposite side of baseline
solutions: Use continuous wave Doppler for very high velocities

PRF.description: Pulse Repetition Frequency - determines maximum velocity measurable
principles: Higher PRF = higher velocities can be measured
Lower PRF = better sensitivity to slow flow
Decrease PRF to see slow venous flow better
settings: Venous exams: low PRF (detect slow flow)
Arterial exams: higher PRF (measure high velocities)

spectralBroadening.description: Widening of spectral waveform, filling of spectral window
causes: Improper sample volume location (too close to wall)
interpretation: Laminar flow = narrow bandwidth, clear spectral window
Turbulent flow = wide bandwidth, filled spectral window
Degree of broadening suggests severity of disturbance

bandwidth.description: Range of frequencies in Doppler signal
characteristics: Narrow bandwidth = laminar flow, single velocity
Wide bandwidth = turbulent flow, range of velocities

accelerationTime.description: Time from onset of systole to peak systolic velocity
normalValues: ICA/cerebral vessels: longer AT than high resistance vessels
AT increases in extremities as distance from heart increases
Measured more easily with increased sweep speed
abnormalValues: AT increases distal to significant stenosis
Decreased cardiac output increases AT bilaterally
Used to differentiate inflow from outflow disease

uses: Evaluates tissue resistance (renal parenchyma, liver, transplants)
Distal occlusion causes increased resistance proximally = high RI

normalValues: Values increase with distance from aorta
uses: Compares PSV-EDV difference to average velocity
Measures variability in blood velocity during cardiac cycle

dampingFactor.description: Describes attenuation of Doppler signal with stenosis
dampingFactor.calculation: Compare PI proximal to PI distal to stenosis

clinical: Slow blood = more pressure on vessel walls
Fast blood (at stenosis) = less pressure on vessel walls
Reduced pressure at stenosis with increased velocity
After stenosis: velocity decreases, pressure increases

plug: Occurs in systole in large vessels

transducers: Linear array: extremities and carotids (5-10 MHz)
Curved/phased array: abdominal and large habitus (2-5 MHz)
Heating above Curie point destroys piezoelectric elements
NO iodine or alcohol cleaners (damages matching layer and adhesives)
presets: Using wrong preset degrades image and extends exam time

kinetic: Varies with mass and velocity squared (KE = ½mv²)
Greater mass or velocity = more kinetic energy
potential: Converts to kinetic energy during flow
gravitational: Stored energy related to elevated position

vesselResistance: Small changes in vessel radius = most significant changes in flow
Increased vessel radius = dramatically decreased resistance
Vessel length also affects resistance but less dramatically

CriticalFindings.title: Critical Findings Requiring Immediate Attention
cerebrovascular: Vertebral artery occlusion with no collaterals
arterial: Acute arterial occlusion (no time for collaterals)
venous: Free-floating thrombus tail (not adhered to wall - high PE risk)
other: Congestive heart failure (CHF) indicated by cardiac pulsatility in lower extremity veins

QuickReference.title: Quick Reference Values

venousVolume: Increases significantly with chronic venous insufficiency
reflux: Other deep veins reflux >1.0 seconds = abnormal

hemodynamicCriteria: 50% diameter stenosis = 75% area stenosis = hemodynamically significant

PatientPositioning.title: Patient Positioning Guide
carotid: Head turned away from side being scanned
Pillow under shoulders helps extend neck
Technologist usually sits at head of bed
lowerExtremityArterial: Leg abducted for medial aspect access
Lateral/decubitus for popliteal fossa and posterior calf
DVTevaluation: Veins more easily visualized when distended
GSVevaluation: Leg rotated outward for medial aspect access

CommonErrors.title: Common Errors to Avoid
stenosisUnderestimation: Most common cause: improper sample volume placement
Must scan through ENTIRE stenotic area
Find highest velocity by moving cursor through stenosis
angleErrors: Angle correction line must be parallel to flow
Cannot measure flow perpendicular to beam (90°)
compressionErrors: Excessive compression may collapse normal vein (false positive)
Must compress every 1-2cm along entire vein
Cannot adequately compress iliac veins due to depth
refluxErrors: Must evaluate reflux in STANDING position
Inadequate compression release may not elicit reflux
Timing: must measure duration accurately (>0.5-1.0 sec)
waveformInterpretation: Cardiac pulsatility in lower extremity veins = CHF (not normal)
Don't confuse respiratory phasicity with cardiac pulsatility
